genZNote: Basically K. pneumoniae's indole-positive sibling — same mucoid vibe, one extra test tells them apart.

habitat.naturalHabitat: Human gastrointestinal tract; also found in soil and water
habitat.hostAssociation: Normal gut flora in some individuals; opportunistic pathogen in healthcare settings
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Found in soil, water, and on plants
habitat.reservoir: Human GI tract and hospital environment

microscopy.appearance: Gram-negative rods, often with a visible capsule (India ink or negative staining)

identificationClues: Gram-negative encapsulated rod, mucoid pink colonies on MacConkey (lactose fermenter)
Indole positive — the key biochemical test that distinguishes it from Klebsiella pneumoniae (indole negative)
Associated with antibiotic-associated hemorrhagic colitis via cytotoxin production

diseases: Antibiotic-associated hemorrhagic colitis (a distinctive association for this species)
virulenceFactors: Cytotoxin production implicated in antibiotic-associated colitis
Can acquire extended-spectrum beta-lactamases and carbapenemases
toxins: Tilivalline — a cytotoxin linked to antibiotic-associated hemorrhagic colitis
clinicalImportance.transmission: Endogenous gut flora; healthcare-associated transmission via hands/devices in hospitalized patients
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: A less common but clinically important cause of nosocomial infections; increasingly reported with multidrug-resistant, carbapenemase-producing strains
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Indole positivity is the standard test distinguishing K. oxytoca from the more common K. pneumoniae

examFacts.importantDisease: UTI, nosocomial pneumonia; antibiotic-associated hemorrhagic colitis
examFacts.importantTest: Indole test (positive) — distinguishes from K. pneumoniae
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: Indole-positive Klebsiella — otherwise very similar to K. pneumoniae but linked to antibiotic-associated colitis via tilivalline toxin
